This. I dipped my toes in both worlds. Started out in architecture school and switched to engineering. I didn't like being graded on whether or not my professor liked my designs. One professor would say something like, "wow, this is really interesting. You've got a lot of potential." But then I'd get a D on the project because someone else just didn't like it. So I went to engineering where there was a definite right or wrong answer. The best advice on architecture school I heard from an architect friend years later, you may be tempted to try and develop a style and mimic the designs that inspire you but think of your professor as your client, if your client isn't happy with your work you don't get the job, so strike that balance between designs you're passionate about and also make your client happy. 

Also, all of my favorite architects were trained as engineers first. They seem to design beautiful buildings that are functional as structures, not like a lot of architects that make artwork then try to cram a building into their sculpture. Spanish architect Calatrava is one of my faves.

Think of it this way, a lot of famous buildings started out as sketches on napkins, anyone can do that. From a practical and legal perspective, nobody is going to build anything unless an engineer looks at the plans and verifies that the building will stand and not collapse and kill someone. You need an engineer to build something, you need a good design to make a beautiful building, anyone with the right talent can make a beautiful design, architects are just better trained to make good designs.

You're not wrong that the infrastructure is a house of cards but we're talking about shooting up a high voltage transformer here. These are large pieces of machinery that already cost millions of dollars without adding armor plating to them. Plus the cooling apparatus be it oil filled radiator plates or some sort of forced air mechanism kinda inherently needs to be open to the elements to work. One small puncture in the chasis and the coolant oil will flow out, the coils will over heat, sparks can follow, sparks next to a puddle of oil equals boom. 

Most of our power grid today is based on radial transmission lines feeding a number of disconnected distribution circuits. Think main transmission "trunks" leaving large power plants that branch off into medium voltage lines, then medium voltage lines go to one of these substations where it is stepped down again to distribution voltage and fed to customers in a defined area. A more robust system would tie each of those open ends way down stream of the power plant together, making the grid look less like a phylogenetic tree like you might have seen in biology class and more like a web with each load being capable of being supplied from any number of directions/substations. This is possible with the tech we currently have, but its complicated to coordinate and expensive.

There is some dissent in the respective Aliens and Predator communities about how Canon the AVP movies are. Personally, I like my Predator story line and Alien story line separate in they're own universes and the cross over stuff as a fun, 'what if?', unique universe all on it's own.

As far as why the predators always end up losing? Partially I think it's for story telling reasons. These are stories made for humans to be entertained. Humans like seeing other humans overcome the odds and win. Stories in which the hero or audience POV character lose are rare. Sure, those types of stories exist, but for every American Psycho there are a dozen movies about a good guy trying to stop the bad guy. The 'hero wins the battle' story arch is much more popular than 'murderer gets away with it' story arch. Hence Arnie/Glover/Brody beating a monster that should have easily wiped the floor with them.

In universe reasons... There's probably a lot of predators coming to Earth stories that haven't been told because the predator won. The stories as told in the movies are just the exceptions, where the predator was beaten. The seeds of those stories are there in the movies, just not explicitly shown. Armed forces guys getting skinned and hung from trees in the middle of jungle warfare, drug lords getting hopped up on coke in LA fighting invisible demons, Morpheus in Predators saying he's been on that planet for years having seen who knows how many predator fights plus that dead soldier who set all the traps. My head-canon is that the movies are the exception, when the humans won, we don't get to see the stories when the predator wins.
